title: Role scripts and fallbacks — Engineering & Platform Audiences
body:
Purpose
---
Working doc for field and SDRs: compact, technical-first scripts and fallback lines when positioning Redwood Inference to three tight audiences — ML engineers, backend engineers, and internal platform teams. Focus: what to say in 3x timeframes (15s, 90s, 10m), what to demo, and how to neutralize common objections (cost, ops burden, model quality).

TL;DR (elevator lines)
- ML engineers (15s): Redwood gives you predictable low-latency inference with built-in KV/prefix caching and model-variant fallbacks — so your evals in prod match dev quality and cost.
- Backend engineers (15s): Same API your app calls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments; predictable throughput and clear cost controls for production traffic.
- Platform teams (15s): One runtime and one set of observability tools to standardize inference across orgs — routing, quotas, and SLAs you can enforce centrally.

90s scripts (core points to deliver)
- ML engineers: "We know you care about reproducible evals and token-level economics. Redwood runs models with runtime-aware kernel selection, automatic KV cache and prefix reuse, and quantization profiles we recommend per workload. That means you keep developer velocity when swapping model versions and get a measurable drop in per-token cost without surprising regressions. Our rollouts support canary evals and automatic fallback to verified variants when latency or quality SLOs break."
- Backend engineers: "If you care about predictable latency and throughput, Redwood exposes a simple REST/SDK interface and manages serving concerns (batching, autoscale, warm pools) so your app threads see consistent p95 latency. You can route by region and tier, attach quotas, and use the Console for token-level cost attribution. No custom scaling logic in your service — just an HTTP call."
- Platform teams: "We provide a single control plane and a private deployment option (VPC/on-prem) so your teams get the same API and observability regardless of where models run. Admins get policy config for routing, quotas, team-level cost limits, and rollback policies — enabling governance without blocking developer autonomy."

Talk tracks: technical hooks and proof points
- Latency & determinism: kernel selection + continuous batching + warm KV caches -> show p50/p95 benchmarks for your common seq-lengths (bring customer sample if possible).
- Cost controls: token-level chargebacks + batching recommendations from Optimize + suggested quantization profiles.
- Quality guardrails: rollout with canary evals, regression alerts tied to your prompt set, and automatic fallback to verified model variants.
- Ops lift reduction: managed warm pools, autoscaling policies, and per-route throttles reduce home-grown orchestration by X FTEs (use case-specific estimate).
- Security & compliance: private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs for enterprise deployments.

Conversation playbook: objection handling
- "We can self-host, why pay?" -> Acknowledge: self-host gives control but costs engineering time. Counter: Redwood reduces ops burden, gives measurable cost-per-token reductions via batching/cache/quantization, and provides validated kernels across hardware to avoid waste. Offer operational savings estimate and migration plan (pilot -> dedicated).
- "Model quality/regression concerns" -> Lead with rollout and eval story: keep canary evals, regression alerts, and the ability to pin versions. Offer a quick A/B plan: 1) mirror a small % of traffic, 2) run prompt-set evals, 3) auto-fallback ON.
- "Latency spikes under load" -> Explain warm pool, capacity tiers, and fallback routing (cheaper model variant or regional failover). Offer a demo showing p95 under concurrency with and without caching.
- "How much work to migrate?" -> Provide a simple migration path: SDK + short config file, an integration checklist (3 API calls, 2 IAM changes, 1 metrics hook), and an SRE-run pilot with dedicated capacity.

Persona-specific demo checklist (10-minute demo mapping)
- ML engineer demo: 1) baseline inference latencies and sample outputs from their model in dev vs Redwood-hosted; 2) show rollout -> canary -> A/B -> automatic fallback; 3) run a small eval suite and show regression alert; 4) show Optimize suggestions (batching/quantization).
- Backend engineer demo: 1) single API call latency/throughput under simulated app load; 2) show quotas & per-route dashboards; 3) illustrate warm pool and autoscale policy change; 4) show token-cost dashboard with attribution by route.
- Platform team demo: 1) multi-team view: assign quotas and alerts; 2) show routing policy by region and tier; 3) private deployment/KMS/enterprise settings; 4) rollout policy enforcing canary across teams.

Competitive positioning notes (concise)
- Versus generalized cloud AI endpoints: emphasize unified runtime + explicit production optimizations (KV caching, continuous batching, kernel selection) — not just a VM + model.
- Versus model-access APIs: emphasize access consistency across hosted/dedicated/private and the operational tooling (rollouts, per-token attribution, fallback policies).
- Versus self-hosted inference stacks: emphasize engineering time saved, validated performance profiles across hardware, and the answer to edge cases (quantization regressions, kernel mismatches).

Metrics & pilot success criteria (example SLA-backed pilot)
- For ML engineers: no >2% regression in key eval metrics on A/B; p95 latency within agreed SLO; regression-alert false positive rate <10%.
- For backend engineers: sustained throughput matching target RPS with p95 latency < target; cost-per-100k-tokens improvement or at least predictable cost per token.
- For platform teams: centralized policy enforcement used by X teams, reduction in bespoke infra for inference, and clear chargeback reporting enabled.

Short email/LinkedIn outreach snippets
- ML engineer subject line: "Quick question — how do you guard production evals when swapping LLMs?" Body lead: "We help teams keep eval fidelity in production with canaries, prompt-set regressions, and automatic model fallbacks. Can I show a 10-minute pilot?"
- Backend engineer subject line: "Reduce inference surprises in production (no infra changes)" Body lead: "Same REST/SDK, predictable p95s — plus warm pools and autoscaling so client threads don't see tail latency surprises. Interested in a 10-minute demo?"
- Platform lead subject line: "Standardize inference: single control plane + per-team quotas" Body lead: "One API, one Console, and policy controls so platform teams can enforce SLAs without slowing devs. Demo slot?"

Example short Slack opening lines (for AE/SEs)
- "Are you seeing any token-cost surprises right now? We often find 10–30% inefficiencies fixed by batching/caching."
- "If you swapped to a new open checkpoint, would you be confident the outputs in prod match your evaluation?"

Open questions & risks (items to resolve before wide rollout)
- Gather: typical seq-length distribution and 95th % concurrency for customer workloads — needed to show concrete p95 numbers.
- Clarify: platform teams' approval process for private deployments (legal & infra timeline).
- Risk: customers conflating "quantization" with quality regressions — we need a one-pager that explains when quantization is recommended and rollback patterns.

Appendix: quick rebut templates (copyable)
- "Quality > cost" -> "We agree. Redwood's rollout + regression alerts give you safety to try quantized variants behind a canary; you can pin high-quality variants for critical routes."
- "We host our own models" -> "Great — Redwood can integrate as a control plane for those self-hosted endpoints or operate as a dedicated tier so you get centralized routing, quotas, and telemetry without rewriting infra."

Notes to self (work items)
- Build p95 demo scripts for sequence lengths: 32, 128, 512.
- Create one-pager: quantization recommendations + rollback recipe.
- Ask product to bake an "ops-savings" calculator for pilot scoping.
